content: Systems thinking examines how components interact within wholes to create emergent properties that individual parts alone cannot explain. Key concepts include interconnectednessâelements within systems influence each other through causal relationships and feedback loops; emergenceâsystems produce behaviors and properties that cannot be predicted from isolated components; nonlinearityâcauses and effects are not proportional, with small changes potentially producing large impacts or vice versa; boundariesâsystems operate within defined scopes with semi-permeable borders allowing exchanges with broader environments; stocks and flowsâsystems contain accumulations (stocks) that change through inflows and outflows over time; and feedback loopsâsystems regulate themselves through reinforcing loops (amplifying changes) and balancing loops (counteracting changes to maintain stability). System archetypes represent recurring patterns across diverse contexts: tragedy of the commons" describes resource depletion when individuals maximize self-interest; "fixes that fail" shows how short-term solutions often create longer-term problems; and "limits to growth" demonstrates how success initially accelerates through reinforcing feedback before encountering constraints that slow progress. Complex adaptive systemsâlike ecosystems, economies, or social networksâfeature additional properties including self-organization (spontaneous order without centralized control), adaptation (changing behavior based on feedback), and coevolution (systems evolving in response to related systems). System leverage points identify where interventions most effectively create change, ranging from shallow leverage (adjusting parameters like taxes or subsidies) to deep leverage (transforming system goals or paradigms). Systems mapping visualizes components and relationships through tools like causal loop diagrams (showing feedback relationships), stock and flow diagrams (tracking accumulations and rates of change), and social network analyses (revealing connection patterns between actors). Systems thinking addresses complex challenges by avoiding reductionism (focusing on parts without context), acknowledging uncertainty and nonlinear dynamics, and considering both intended and unintended consequences of interventions.

scenario.title: Event Planning Network
scenario.content: Students organize a virtual school dance by managing interconnected systems including venue logistics, entertainment, refreshments, decorations, promotion, and budgeting. The simulation reveals relationships between seemingly separate decisions, showing how choices in one area create ripple effects throughout the event system. Students can manipulate different variables and observe how changes propagateâadjusting the venue size affects capacity, which influences ticket pricing, impacting budget for entertainment and refreshments, ultimately affecting attendance and participant experience. The system visualizes causal connections through interactive maps showing feedback loops, time delays, and emergent behaviors that arise from component interactions. Interactive tools demonstrate systems concepts like stocks and flows (tracking resources, attendance, and satisfaction), reinforcing and balancing feedback (promotional buzz versus capacity constraints), and unintended consequences (how cost-cutting in one area might decrease overall experience). Challenge scenarios introduce disruptions like budget changes, venue problems, or schedule conflicts that require adaptive responses and systems-level thinking to maintain event success.

hypothesis.description: Students will apply systems thinking by mapping relationships between components in complex situations. They will predict how changes propagate through interconnected elements, and design interventions that leverage system structure to achieve desired outcomes while minimizing unintended consequences.
